regions.name: Red Centre and Outback
visual_identifiers: very flat terrain with occasional low scrub
intense blue sky with no clouds
very long straight roads to horizon

state_distinguishers.NT_vs_WA_outback: NT has more red rock escarpments. WA outback more flat red sandy desert. NT has distinctive Darwin-area tropical top end.
state_distinguishers.Uluru_area: Distinctive red rock monoliths = almost certainly Northern Territory.

regions.route_sign_clues: NT uses black and white signs. WA uses specific green signs. Road names often include Stuart Highway, Nullarbor. IMPORTANT: Route numbers alone (A1, A87 etc) do not confirm a state — the same number formats are used nationally.
regions.gemini_hint: Red dirt + spinifex grass = Australian outback. Uluru-style red rock = Northern Territory. Termite mounds = NT or northern WA. Do not use road numbers alone to distinguish NT from outback WA or SA.
common_false_positives: Route numbers like A1, A87 — same format used in all outback states
Red dirt road — present in NT, outback WA, outback SA and outback QLD
Flat featureless terrain — applies equally to outback WA, SA and QLD
Sparse dry scrub — common across all four outback states

regions.name: Tropical North Queensland

state_distinguishers.Far_North_vs_Southeast_QLD: Far north tropical and lush. Southeast Queensland more subtropical and developed near Brisbane.

regions.route_sign_clues: Queensland uses specific yellow and black route markers historically. IMPORTANT: Do not use a route number alone to confirm Queensland — verify the sign colour and shape.
regions.gemini_hint: Sugarcane fields + tropical vegetation = North Queensland. Cassowary warning sign = Far North Queensland confirmed. Lush tropical green alone is not enough — it also appears in northern NT and far north WA.
common_false_positives: Lush green tropical vegetation — also present in Darwin/NT Top End
Queensland route numbers — the number itself is not unique; confirm by sign colour (yellow/black)
Rainforest — also present in northern NSW and parts of NT

regions.name: Southeast Australia
visual_identifiers: specific NSW and Victorian road signs
blue mountains visible west of Sydney

state_distinguishers.NSW_vs_Victoria: NSW signs are blue and yellow. Victorian signs are green and yellow. Victoria has more English-feeling countryside in some areas. IMPORTANT: Both states have tall eucalyptus and mountain ash forests — tall straight trees alone do NOT confirm WA over Victoria or NSW.
state_distinguishers.ACT: Canberra distinctive planned city layout, wide boulevards, specific ACT government signage.
state_distinguishers.Victoria_tall_forests: Victoria's Otway Ranges, Dandenong Ranges and East Gippsland contain very tall mountain ash and messmate forests. These can look similar to WA karri. Sign colour (green/yellow = Victoria) is the reliable distinguisher.

regions.route_sign_clues: NSW uses blue and yellow distinctive signs. Victoria uses green and yellow. These are very reliable state identifiers. IMPORTANT: Route numbers like A440 exist in both Victoria and WA — never use a route number alone to confirm the state.
regions.gemini_hint: Blue and yellow road signs = New South Wales. Green and yellow road signs = Victoria. This colour difference is very reliable. Tall straight forest alone is NOT enough — both Victoria and WA have tall straight forests. Look for sign colour.
common_false_positives: A440 route number — also exists in Western Australia; do not use alone
Tall straight trees / mountain ash forest — present in Victoria (Otways, Dandenongs, East Gippsland) as well as WA
Temperate eucalyptus forest — common across NSW, Victoria, SA and WA
Green rolling hills — present in both Victoria and NSW; not a distinguisher between the two
General Ax/Bx route numbers — same format used nationally

regions.name: Western Australia Coast
visual_identifiers: southwest has distinctive karri and jarrah forests
specific red gravel roads in places

state_distinguishers.Southwest_WA: Karri forest (very tall straight trees) is distinctive of southwest WA, BUT similar tall forests exist in Victoria (Otway Ranges, East Gippsland) and Tasmania. Confirm with WA-specific green road signs, not just tree height.
state_distinguishers.Perth_area: Large modern Australian city with specific infrastructure.

regions.route_sign_clues: WA uses specific green road signs. IMPORTANT: Route numbers like A1, A9, A440 exist in MULTIPLE Australian states. Do NOT use a route number alone to identify WA unless the sign format or colour is also visible and matches WA specifically. The South Western Highway (WA) is signed as State Route 1 in official signage, not just a painted number. A440 painted on a road does not confirm WA — A440 also exists in Victoria.
regions.gemini_hint: Very tall straight karri or jarrah forest COMBINED WITH WA-specific green road signs = Southwest Western Australia. Tall straight trees alone are NOT sufficient — Victoria and Tasmania also have very tall straight forests. Always require a second confirming clue (sign colour, WA-specific infrastructure) before assigning WA.
common_false_positives: A440 road number — also exists in Victoria (Geelong area); do not use alone to confirm WA
Tall straight trees — karri/jarrah in WA but mountain ash and messmate equally tall in Victoria's Otway Ranges and East Gippsland
Dry eucalyptus forest — common across SA, WA, NSW and Victoria
General green road signs — used in multiple states; WA sign shape/format must be specifically identifiable
General Ax/Bx route numbers — same format used nationally, not WA-specific

regions.name: South Australia and Tasmania
visual_identifiers: SA: dry Mediterranean scrub around Adelaide

state_distinguishers.Tasmania_vs_mainland: Tasmania looks distinctly different — much greener, more English countryside feel, older convict-era architecture. However, tall green forest alone does not confirm Tasmania over Victoria.
state_distinguishers.SA_wine_regions: Barossa and Clare Valley have distinctive European-influenced winery architecture.

regions.route_sign_clues: Tasmania has distinctive Tasmanian devil on some signs. SA uses specific sign formats. IMPORTANT: Do not use route numbers alone to confirm SA or Tasmania — verify sign shape and colour.
regions.gemini_hint: Very green English countryside feel in Australia = almost certainly Tasmania. Flat dry scrub with Mediterranean feel near city = South Australia. NOTE: Green temperate forest alone is not sufficient for Tasmania — Victoria also has green temperate forest. Look for older architecture, narrower roads, and the distinct Tasmanian feel.
common_false_positives: Green temperate forest — also present in Victoria and parts of NSW; not Tasmania-specific alone
English countryside feel — also possible in parts of Victoria (Yarra Valley, Dandenongs)
Flat terrain — present in SA, WA, QLD and parts of NSW; not SA-specific
General Ax/Bx route numbers — same format used nationally
